# Worksheet: Finding the Real Replicate

[📥 Littoraria data](data/littoraria.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="littoraria.csv"} [📥 Tools script (.R)](themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R){.btn .btn-primary download="r_themes_and_functions.R"} [📥 Script skeleton (.R)](09_study_design_homework.R){.btn .btn-primary download="09_study_design_homework.R"}

**The study.** *Littoraria angulifera* is a mangrove periwinkle found on both sides of the tropical Atlantic. Gotelli & Ellison's dataset holds shell measurements from **1022 snails** collected at **18 sites** — nine on the East Atlantic coast of Africa, nine on the West Atlantic coast of the Americas.

**The question.** Are West Atlantic snails bigger than East Atlantic snails?

**In class** you took a small, tidy, balanced experiment and asked whether one of its treatment arms earned its place. **This is the same workflow on a dataset that is none of those things** — 1022 rows, wildly uneven sampling, and nobody assigned anything to anything. One decision in Part 2 determines whether you get the right answer, and the data will not warn you if you get it wrong.

Columns: `site`, `coast`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `shell_breadth_mm`, `shell_height_mm`, `aperture_length_mm`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 1 · Setup and the data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)

snail_df
```

# Part 3 · The analysis almost everyone runs first

**▶ Run this** — every snail treated as an independent replicate:

``` r

t.test(shell_breadth_mm ~ coast, data = snail_df)
```

# Part 4 · The analysis the design actually calls for

**▶ Run this** — collapse to one number per site first, then test:

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · The analysis the design actually calls for ───────────────
site_df <- snail_df %>%
  group_by(coast, site) %>%
  summarise(mean_breadth = mean(shell_breadth_mm), n_snails = n(), .groups = "drop")

site_df
```

# Part 5 · Why they disagree

**▶ Run this** — the standard error at each level:

``` r

snail_df %>%
  group_by(coast) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(shell_breadth_mm))

site_df %>%
  group_by(coast) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(mean_breadth))
```

# Part 7 · The figure you hand in

The only plot with labels, a theme and a title. Show **both levels at once** so the reader can see where the uncertainty actually lives.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(site_df, aes(coast, mean_breadth)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(size = n_snails), width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.4, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Shell breadth of Littoraria angulifera by coast",
    subtitle = "One point per site (n = 9 per coast); point size is snails sampled",
    x = "Coast",
    y = "Mean shell breadth (mm)",
    size = "Snails"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/littoraria_figure.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 6,
  height = 4,
  units  = "in"
)
```

# Review and checkpoint

At this point you can:

- [ ] Find every candidate level of replication in a dataset before testing anything
- [ ] Choose the level that matches the question, and justify it
- [ ] Recognise that pseudoreplication shrinks the SE rather than changing the means
- [ ] Say what an unbalanced sampling effort does to a pooled estimate
- [ ] Name a confounder in a natural experiment and decide whether adjusting for it is appropriate
